content.p: "Albanian mafia" is the name police, prosecutors and newspapers give to a loose set of criminal groups that are based in Albania or made up of ethnic Albanians. The groups are not a single organization with one leader and one structure. Most of what is known about them comes from court cases, police operations and investigative reporting, and the sources often disagree about how large the groups are, how much money they make and how much control they have over particular markets.

Since the 1990s, Albanian-speaking networks have moved heroin, cocaine, cannabis and ecstasy across Europe and into the United States, and have been linked by police to prostitution and human trafficking. The story runs from clan-based drug smuggling in the Balkans, through Italian and Dutch ports, to London street gangs and the coordinated arrests of the 2010s and 2020s.
content.h2: Origins in the Balkan heroin trade
content.p: Mother Jones, writing in January 2000 after the Kosovo war, described Kosovar Albanian smugglers as among the world's most experienced dealers in contraband, operating from isolated ports and mountain villages. The magazine said that much of the Balkan heroin business was directed by a loose hierarchy it called "The 15 Families", which answered to regional clans. That is a 2000 journalistic description, and the magazine presented it as reporting rather than as a court finding.

The same article reported that the clans had maintained an armed brigade that gradually evolved into the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA). It cited a congressional briefing paper which said that "between 30 and 50 percent" of the KLA's money might come from drugs, and it said the paper's authors had described such allegations as something that could not be dismissed. The magazine also quoted German Federal Police saying that Kosovar Albanians imported 80 percent of Europe's heroin. These were claims made in 2000, not findings of a court.

In Mother Jones's account, heroin from Afghanistan passed through Iran to Turkey, where it was refined, and then reached the border towns linking Macedonia, Albania and Serbia. When the Bosnian war closed the direct road through Yugoslavia, two splinter routes developed, according to Mother Jones.

Albanian crime became consolidated in several Italian regions. In a 2017 article, exit.al quoted a report by the Italian anti-mafia directorate, known as the DIA, which had warned about 2000 of "clans that had a mafioso character" taking root in territory that Italian crime had left behind. The DIA's 2016 report counted 280 Albanians in Italian prisons for mafia-type offenses, second only to Romanians. It also said that Puglia remained a compulsory entry point for illegal traffic from Albania.

The operations were often built around family ties. In one case reported by OCCRP, Italian police arrested 33 Albanians on the Adriatic coast after an investigation that began with a 2.5-kilo cocaine sale in 2011 to two men the police said were alleged members of a Camorra clan. The Carabinieri in Chieti said the group worked from Abruzzo, where they believed a local mafia was absent, and that the key suspect, a 35-year-old man, worked with his mother, sister-in-law and several uncles. The prosecutors charged seven of the 33 with mafia-type association and said nine more were still at large. OCCRP reported that the group allegedly sold heroin for about 12,000 euros a kilo, half the average price in Italy.

The Carabinieri officer quoted by OCCRP described the group as "very mobile", saying such groups stayed about ten years in one country before moving on. That is one investigator's view, not a measured fact about every group.
content.h2: Operation Black Eagle in the United States
content.p: The FBI ran a four-year joint investigation in the New Jersey and New York area, code-named Black Eagle after the Albanian flag. The FBI's Newark office, which announced the charges in 2009, said the joint work had started in late 2003 with targets in six other countries, among them Albania, Macedonia and Serbia.

The FBI said 26 people were charged with narcotics and firearms trafficking, money laundering, interstate transport of stolen property and conspiracy. Seventeen were arrested over five days in cities including Paterson, Lodi, Clifton and Wayne in New Jersey, and in Brooklyn and Staten Island. Agents who infiltrated the group bought large amounts of ecstasy and heroin, and the FBI described negotiations that covered cocaine and other drugs from Canada, Greece, Macedonia, Albania, Turkey and Serbia. The agency said the case showed that the defendants "had links to criminal associates in seven countries". The FBI called the charges accusations and said every defendant was presumed innocent.

Two of the men the FBI sought were Kujtim "Timmy" Lika and Myfit "Mike" Dika. Lika was on the FBI's Most Wanted list and was arrested in Toronto, according to OCCRP, which reported that he and two associates had fled to Canada. Dika was arrested by a fugitive task force in Toronto in January 2010, and a third fugitive, Gazmir Gjoka, was arrested in Albania in November 2009. The special agent who led the operation, Jim Farley, told OCCRP that the whole organization was "about 24 strong", a figure that differs from the 26 the FBI charged. OCCRP also quoted Farley saying the group's heroin sales were concentrated in northern New Jersey and New York, with ties to Chicago, Detroit and Texas, and international ties to Macedonia and Albania.
The final outcome of the individual cases against Lika, Dika or Gjoka is not reported in the accounts quoted above. Their charges should be read as accusations.

From the mid-2010s, police in several countries began to describe Albanian groups as major cocaine importers, not only cannabis and heroin distributors. The Independent reported in 2019 that Albania had become a major route for cannabis into the European Union, and that traffickers had moved into cocaine after the government's crackdown on cannabis growing. The paper argued that the traffickers' profits could buy influence at ports as far apart as Rotterdam and Izmir.

The Guardian's 2019 investigation of the UK market described the Albanian groups as having negotiated directly with Colombian cartels rather than buying through separate importers and wholesalers. Intelligence it reported put the price the Albanians paid at about £4,000 to £5,500 a kilo, while rivals were said to be buying from Dutch wholesalers at about £22,500 a kilo. A former head of drugs intelligence at the National Crime Agency, Tony Saggers, told the paper that the groups were giving a good slice of their margins to customers. The Guardian reported the National Crime Agency's belief that Albanian groups were consolidating their hold on the UK cocaine market, which it put at £5bn.

The Guardian also reported that Albanian groups worked with the 'Ndrangheta, a group with roots in southern Italy, to control ports. Anna Sergi, a criminologist at the University of Essex, told the paper that when the 'Ndrangheta shipped goods, "they work a lot with the Albanians". The newspaper said that the Belgian and Dutch ports of Antwerp and Rotterdam, which are among Europe's largest, were key points where Albanian groups were expanding their influence. These are the paper's findings and the views it quoted; they were not tested in court in the article.
content.h2: Kompania Bello and Operation Los Blancos
content.p: In September 2020, police arrested 20 suspects in raids in 10 countries in Europe and the Middle East. The operation, codenamed Los Blancos, followed a five-year investigation led by prosecutors in Florence. Europol called it the biggest of its kind against Albanian-speaking organized crime. Balkan Insight, working with court documents, reported that the prosecutors described the target group, Kompania Bello, as a "transnational crime federation" of 14 Albanian crime organizations operating from at least 2014 across Ecuador, the Netherlands, Belgium, Albania and Italy.

The prosecutors identified Dritan Rexhepi, who is 40 years old in the report, as the "undisputed 'capo'" of the group. Balkan Insight reported that he had been sentenced to 25 years in absentia by a Tirana court in 2013 for two murders in 1998, one of the victims a police officer, and that he had a record of convictions for cocaine trafficking in Italy and armed robbery in Belgium. In 2014 he was arrested in Quito, Ecuador, in a police bust that seized 278 kilograms of cocaine. The report said he was serving a 13-year sentence and was still wanted in Albania, Italy and Belgium. He is accused, by Albanian authorities, of ordering from prison an abduction in central Albania; the victim has not been found, and Rexhepi told a journalist he had never been involved in kidnapping or contract killings. Italian prosecutors also accused him of ordering at least two other murders while in prison.

The same report described how the group used encrypted communications to organize couriers and recruitment, and how a network of corrupt officials was said to have monitored cargo at ports. Balkan Insight quoted an Albanian prosecutor who spoke anonymously saying that the group enforced "a pact of silence" among members who were arrested. Those are prosecutors' allegations, and the reporting gives no verdicts against most of the people named.
content.h2: the UK and the street trade
content.p: In London, the Guardian's 2019 reporting described a gang called Hellbanianz as the street-level dealers and enforcers of the wider Albanian network, which police sources placed at the lowest rung of that hierarchy. The paper quoted the National Crime Agency's view that the Albanian groups were close to a near-total takeover of the UK cocaine market, while the gang itself was known locally for violence and for social media posts that displayed cash, cars and watches.
content.h2: Albania, cannabis and the drug wars at home
content.p: The trafficking networks are also a problem inside Albania. The Independent reported in 2019 that some estimated the country's cannabis trade at up to $4bn a year, about half of Albania's GDP, a figure it attributed to estimates rather than official accounts. Albanian officials conceded they intercepted only about 10 per cent of shipments, and one Western diplomat put it closer to 5 per cent. The paper quoted a diplomat describing the country as "the Colombia of Europe".

Balkan Insight reported that Shkurti, also known as Aldo Bare, led a group that took its name from the town of Lushnja, and that he had been accused in 1997 of decapitating a rival, Artur Daja. Shkurti was arrested in Ankara in March 2006 and extradited to Albania in November 2009. Prosecutors in Tirana charged him with five murders, organizing a criminal group, and international drug trafficking. In March 2011 Balkan Insight reported that he had been sentenced to life in prison. The group's intimidation was said to reach the police, the secret services and politicians.

Albanian journalist Artan Hoxha, quoted by the Independent, said there had been increasing competition between rival drug gangs, and that about 23 people linked to the drug trade had disappeared over a year. The Independent also reported that Hoxha received a death threat after a television broadcast, the caller was anonymous.

The sources disagree on almost every number. Black Eagle's FBI count of 26 defendants differs from the "about 24" given by an agent to OCCRP. Mother Jones, in 2000, quoted German Federal Police on an 80 percent share of Europe's heroin for Kosovar Albanians, a figure no court has tested in these sources. The Guardian's cocaine prices come from intelligence it reported, and the Independent's cannabis value is an estimate. Of the 64 arrests in Europol's 2019 operation, 55 were in Belgium, seven in the Netherlands and two in France; the investigation also involved Italy's anti-mafia directorate and the UK's Metropolitan Police, as exit.al reported in April 2019. In August 2025 Albanian police arrested 10 suspected members of a network that Europol said was involved in cocaine shipments to Hamburg and Rotterdam. OCCRP reported that the leader had reportedly earned more than $40 million from one shipment, a figure reported by OCCRP rather than established by a verdict.

Police operations in 2019, 2020 and 2025 show that Albanian-speaking networks are still a target in Belgium, France, the Netherlands, Italy, the UK, Albania and beyond. Where courts have decided cases, the outcomes involve particular people, not the groups as a whole. The label "Albanian mafia" covers many separate networks, some of them rivals, and most of the claims about their size, profits and political reach remain disputed.
